Our Physiotherapy Services in Milton

General Physiotherapy

Comprehensive musculoskeletal assessment and treatment for pain, injuries, surgery recovery, and mobility improvement. Our physiotherapists use manual therapy, therapeutic exercise, electrotherapy, and education to restore function and prevent recurrence.

Registered Massage Therapy

Therapeutic massage for muscle tension, stress relief, sports recovery, and chronic pain management. Available modalities include deep tissue massage, Swedish massage, hot stone massage, sports massage, prenatal massage, and lymphatic drainage.

Manual Osteopathy

Gentle, hands-on treatment that restores balance to your musculoskeletal system. Manual osteopathy addresses joint restrictions, tissue tension, and circulatory issues to reduce pain and improve whole-body function.

Shockwave Therapy

Advanced non-invasive treatment for chronic tendon conditions including plantar fasciitis, tennis elbow, golfer's elbow, calcific shoulder tendinitis, and Achilles tendinopathy. Break through plateaus when other treatments have stalled.

Motor Vehicle Accident Rehabilitation

Complete MVA recovery programs for whiplash, soft tissue injuries, concussions, and post-traumatic pain. We coordinate directly with your insurance provider and handle all documentation so you can focus on healing.

WSIB Care Programs

Workplace injury treatment and return-to-work planning approved by the Workplace Safety and Insurance Board. From initial assessment to functional capacity evaluation, we guide injured workers through every step of recovery.

Custom Orthotics

Professional gait analysis and custom-fitted orthotic devices to correct biomechanical issues, reduce foot and knee pain, and improve alignment. Covered by most extended health insurance plans.

Custom and OTC Bracing

Expert fitting for knee braces, ankle supports, back braces, and compression garments. Custom options available for post-surgical recovery and complex joint instability.

Compression Therapy

Medical-grade compression socks and sleeves for circulation support, edema management, and athletic recovery. Proper fitting by trained professionals.

TMJ Treatment

Specialized jaw pain and temporomandibular joint dysfunction treatment. Manual therapy, exercises, and modalities to relieve clicking, locking, and chronic facial pain.

B-Pulse Pelvic Floor Strengthening

Non-invasive, clothed pelvic floor rehabilitation using electromagnetic technology. Effective for incontinence, postpartum recovery, and pelvic weakness in men and women.

Frequently Asked Questions

FAQs About Registered Massage Therapy​

What is Orthopedic Physiotherapy?

Orthopedic physiotherapy is focused on treating conditions and injuries affecting the bones, joints, muscles, and connective tissues. It includes a range of treatments to help reduce pain, improve movement, and prevent further injury or deterioration.

How can Orthopedic Physiotherapy help me?

Orthopedic physiotherapy can help relieve pain, improve joint and muscle function, and promote healing from injuries or surgeries. It’s particularly effective for treating sprains, fractures, arthritis, and back or neck pain. Physiotherapists use a variety of techniques including manual therapy, exercises, and modalities to improve function and reduce discomfort.

When should I see an Orthopedic Physiotherapist?

You should consult an orthopedic physiotherapist if you are experiencing pain, stiffness, or difficulty with movement in your joints, muscles, or bones. It is also beneficial after surgery, an injury, or for managing chronic conditions like arthritis. Early intervention can help improve recovery time and prevent long-term complications.

What happens during an Orthopedic Physiotherapy session?

During your session, the physiotherapist will assess your condition and create a treatment plan. This typically includes exercises to improve strength, flexibility, and mobility, along with manual therapy techniques to alleviate pain. They may also educate you on posture, ergonomics, and self-care strategies to prevent further injury.

How long will I need Orthopedic Physiotherapy?

The length of treatment depends on your specific condition and recovery goals. Some individuals may need only a few sessions, while others with more complex or chronic conditions may require ongoing treatment. Your physiotherapist will monitor your progress and adjust the plan as needed.

FAQs About Our TMJ Treatment​ Service In Milton

What is TMJ treatment?

TMJ treatment addresses pain and dysfunction in the jaw joint and surrounding muscles. At Tonic Physio, it may include manual therapy, soft tissue release, joint mobilizations, and corrective exercises.

How long is each TMJ session?

Sessions typically last 30 to 60 minutes, depending on your needs and treatment plan.

How many sessions will I need?

It depends on the severity of your symptoms. Some people feel better in a few visits, while others benefit from ongoing care and maintenance.

What’s the best treatment for TMJ dysfunction?

The best treatment depends on your symptoms. Our physiotherapists use a combination of techniques to reduce pain, improve jaw mobility, and support long-term recovery from TMJ dysfunction.

What are the most common symptoms of TMJ dysfunction (TMD)?

Common symptoms of TMJ dysfunction include localized jaw pain, a clicking, popping, or grating sound when chewing or speaking, restricted jaw movement (lockjaw), and difficulty chewing. Many patients also experience secondary symptoms like earaches, dizziness, or facial pain.

How do I know if my jaw pain is TMJ?

If your jaw pain is accompanied by stiffness, clicking sounds when opening your mouth, or pain that radiates to your face and neck, it is highly likely related to the temporomandibular joint. A comprehensive assessment by one of our physiotherapists can accurately diagnose the root cause of your pain.

Can TMJ cause headaches and neck pain?

Yes, absolutely. The muscles surrounding your temporomandibular joint are closely connected to your neck and head. When there is tension, dysfunction, or misalignment in the jaw, it often radiates, leading to severe tension headaches, migraines, and chronic neck and shoulder stiffness. Treating the TMJ often resolves these secondary pains.

 

Can TMJ cause ear pain or ringing (tinnitus)?

Yes. Because the temporomandibular joint sits just in front of the ear, inflammation and muscle spasms in the jaw can cause referred pain to the ear, a feeling of fullness, or even ringing in the ears (tinnitus).

What causes TMJ disorders?

TMJ issues can stem from a variety of factors. The most common causes include teeth grinding or clenching (bruxism) often due to stress, poor posture (especially "forward head" posture from desk work), arthritis in the joint, or direct trauma/injury to the jaw or face.

Can physiotherapy permanently cure TMJ?

Physiotherapy is highly effective at resolving TMJ symptoms for the vast majority of patients. While the ability to completely "cure" it depends on the underlying cause (such as degenerative arthritis vs. muscular tension), our targeted manual therapy, dry needling, and posture correction techniques provide long-lasting relief and give you the tools to prevent future flare-ups.

Are there exercises I can do at home for TMJ relief?

Yes! A crucial part of our TMJ treatment at Tonic Physiotherapy involves empowering you with a customized home exercise program. We will teach you specific, gentle jaw stretches, strengthening exercises, and relaxation techniques to reduce tension and improve your jaw's range of motion between clinic visits.

Do I need a doctor's referral for TMJ physiotherapy?

No, you do not need a doctor's referral to see a physiotherapist for TMJ treatment. You can book an assessment directly with our clinic. However, some extended health insurance plans may require a physician's note for reimbursement, so it is best to check your specific policy.

Managing Cervical Spondylosis: Specialized Neck Care in Milton

Cervical spondylosis is a term used to describe the age-related wear and tear of the spinal discs in your neck. While it is a common part of aging, it does not have to mean living with chronic stiffness, headaches, and limited range of motion. At Tonic Physio, we provide targeted interventions to manage the symptoms of cervical spondylosis and restore the fluid movement of your neck.

What Exactly is Cervical Spondylosis?

Unlike a sudden injury, spondylosis is a degenerative process. Over time, the discs between the vertebrae in the neck lose water and elasticity. This can lead to the formation of bone spurs (osteophytes) and the thickening of ligaments, which can narrow the space for the nerves exiting the spine.

The Progression of Neck Degeneration

It often starts with a subtle stiffness in the morning. As it progresses, you may notice: * A grinding or popping sound when turning your head. * A reduced ability to look over your shoulder while driving. * Persistent tension in the shoulders and upper back. * Occasional tingling in the fingers or weakness in the hands.

The "Tech Neck" Connection

While spondylosis is degenerative, modern habits accelerate the process. Spending hours looking down at a smartphone or leaning into a laptop screen puts immense pressure on the cervical vertebrae. This chronic strain speeds up the wear and tear on the discs, making spondylosis appear in younger populations than ever before.

How Tonic Physio Treats Cervical Spondylosis

You cannot reverse the aging of a disc, but you can absolutely change how that disc affects your life. We focus on improving the mechanical function of the neck and reducing the pressure on the surrounding nerves.

Manual Therapy for Joint Decompression

Stiffness in the cervical spine is often the result of "locked" joints. Our therapists use gentle, controlled mobilizations to improve the glide of the vertebrae. This helps reduce the pressure on the nerve roots and eases the tension in the surrounding muscles, providing immediate relief from stiffness.

Soft Tissue Release and Trigger Point Therapy

Spondylosis often causes the muscles in the neck and upper traps to work overtime to stabilize the joint. This leads to painful knots and chronic tension. We use targeted soft tissue work to release these trigger points, improving blood flow and reducing the "heavy" feeling in your shoulders.

Postural Correction and Ergonomic Training

The neck does not exist in a vacuum; it is heavily influenced by the position of your ribcage and shoulders. We analyze your overall posture to ensure your neck is not compensating for a rounded upper back. We provide specific training on: * Optimal monitor height to keep the gaze neutral. * Support strategies for long periods of sitting. * Dynamic movement breaks to prevent the "frozen" feeling in the neck.

Therapeutic Exercise and Strengthening

Stability is the best defense against degeneration. We implement a phased exercise program: * Range of Motion: Gentle movements to maintain the current flexibility. * Deep Neck Flexor Strengthening: Training the muscles that support the vertebrae from the inside. * Scapular Stability: Strengthening the shoulder blades to provide a solid foundation for the neck.

Managing the Secondary Effects of Spondylosis

Cervical spondylosis rarely stays confined to the neck. It often triggers a chain reaction of symptoms that affect your overall quality of life.

Addressing Cervicogenic Headaches

When the joints in the upper neck are stiff, they can refer pain upward into the skull. This results in cervicogenic headaches, which often feel like a band tightening around the head or a dull ache at the base of the skull. By treating the neck, we can significantly reduce the frequency and intensity of these headaches.

Improving Sleep Quality

Many people with spondylosis struggle to find a comfortable sleeping position. The wrong pillow can put the neck in a position of excessive flexion or extension, leading to morning stiffness and pain. We offer guidance on pillow selection and sleep positioning to ensure your neck recovers while you sleep.

Preventing Neurological Decline

In advanced cases, spondylosis can lead to myelopathy (compression of the spinal cord). We monitor for signs of coordination loss or balance issues, ensuring that our treatment remains safe and effective while coordinating with medical specialists when necessary.

Living Well With a Degenerative Spine

A diagnosis of cervical spondylosis is not a sentence to a life of pain. With the right management, most people can maintain a high level of function and avoid the need for surgical intervention.

The Importance of Consistent Mobility

The "use it or lose it" principle applies heavily to the neck. Regular, gentle mobility work prevents the bone spurs from causing excessive restriction. We help you build a 5 minute daily routine that keeps your neck fluid and responsive.

Hydration and Disc Health

Like the lumbar discs, cervical discs rely on hydration to maintain their height and cushioning. Staying hydrated and maintaining a healthy diet supports the remaining disc tissue and reduces the risk of further degeneration.

FAQs About Cervical Spondylosis

 

Is cervical spondylosis the same as a herniated disc?

No. A herniated disc is a specific event where the disc wall tears. Spondylosis is a general term for the wear and tear (osteoarthritis) of the spine. However, spondylosis can eventually lead to disc herniation.

Can this condition be cured?

Degenerative changes cannot be "undone" because you cannot regrow a disc. However, the symptoms can be managed so effectively that they no longer interfere with your daily life. We treat the function, not just the X-ray.

Will I eventually need surgery?

The vast majority of people with cervical spondylosis do not need surgery. Surgery is typically reserved for cases where there is severe spinal cord compression or failure of conservative treatments. Physiotherapy is the first and most effective line of defense.

Why does my arm feel numb if the problem is in my neck?

The nerves that control your arms and hands exit from the cervical spine. If a bone spur or a degenerated disc compresses these nerves in the neck, you feel the symptoms in your arm or hand. This is known as referred pain.

Can I still exercise with cervical spondylosis?

Yes, and you should. Exercise increases blood flow to the joints and strengthens the muscles that support the spine. However, certain movements, like heavy overhead presses or high-impact jumping, may need to be modified.

How do I know if my headaches are caused by my neck?

Cervicogenic headaches usually start at the base of the skull and move forward. They are often triggered by certain neck positions or long periods of stillness. A physiotherapy assessment can confirm if your neck is the source of your headaches.

Targeted Sciatica Relief: Expert Sciatica Treatment in Milton

Sciatica is not a diagnosis in itself, but a symptom of an underlying issue. It is the radiating pain, tingling, or numbness that travels along the sciatic nerve, from your lower back through your hips and down each leg. This sensation can range from a mild ache to a debilitating electric shock that makes walking or sitting nearly impossible. At Tonic Physio, we dig deeper to find the root cause of your nerve irritation and implement a strategy to shut down the pain.

Identifying the Source of Sciatic Pain

Because the sciatic nerve is the longest and widest nerve in the human body, the source of the irritation can be in several different places. To treat sciatica effectively, we must first determine where the nerve is being compressed.

Lumbar Disc Issues

The most common cause of sciatica is a herniated or bulging disc in the lower spine. When the disc presses against the nerve root, it triggers the classic "shooting" pain down the leg. This often feels worse when you bend forward or sit for long periods.

Piriformis Syndrome

The sciatic nerve runs directly under (and sometimes through) the piriformis muscle in the buttock. If this muscle becomes tight or spasms, it can pinch the nerve. This type of sciatica is often felt more intensely in the gluteal region and can be aggravated by sitting in a hard chair.

Spinal Stenosis

As we age, the spaces within our spine can narrow. This narrowing, known as stenosis, can put pressure on the nerve roots. Sciatica caused by stenosis often feels better when leaning forward (like leaning on a shopping cart) and worse when standing straight or walking.

Spondylolisthesis

This occurs when one vertebra slips forward over another, potentially pinching the nerve. This often presents as instability in the lower back coupled with radiating leg pain.

The Tonic Physio Protocol for Sciatica Recovery

We move beyond temporary fixes like heat pads and painkillers. Our goal is to decompression the nerve and stabilize the joints to prevent the pain from returning.

Immediate Nerve Desensitization

When a nerve is "angry," it becomes hyper-sensitive to movement. Our first priority is to calm the nerve. We use gentle mobilization techniques and specific positioning to create space for the nerve to glide without irritation. This reduces the "electric" feeling and allows the patient to move more freely.

Manual Therapy and Joint Mobilization

We use targeted manual therapy to address the source of the compression. If the issue is joint-based, we mobilize the vertebrae to restore normal movement. If the issue is muscular, such as Piriformis Syndrome, we use soft tissue release and trigger point therapy to relax the muscle and free the nerve.

Nerve Gliding and Flossing

Nerves need to slide smoothly through the tissues of the body. When inflammation occurs, nerves can get "stuck." We teach our patients "nerve flossing" techniques—gentle, rhythmic movements that stretch and release the nerve, improving its mobility and reducing the sensitivity of the nervous system.

Strategic Strengthening

Pain often leads to "inhibited" muscles, meaning your brain stops firing the muscles that actually protect your back. We use a phased strengthening approach: 1. Activation: Waking up the deep core and glutes. 2. Stabilization: Learning to hold the spine steady during leg movements. 3. Functional Load: Returning to the activities you love, such as hiking, lifting, or sports, with a resilient back.

Breaking the Cycle of Chronic Nerve Pain

Sciatica often follows a cycle: pain leads to inactivity, inactivity leads to stiffness, and stiffness leads to more pain. Breaking this cycle requires a balanced approach of movement and recovery.

The Danger of Total Bed Rest

Old medical advice suggested bed rest for sciatica. We now know that too much rest makes the muscles stiffen and the nerves more sensitive. Our approach is "relative rest"—avoiding the specific movements that trigger the pain while staying active in ways that promote healing.

Ergonomic Adjustments for Nerve Relief

Your environment plays a huge role in how your nerve recovers. We analyze your daily habits: * The Office Chair: How to support the lumbar curve to prevent disc pressure. * Sleep Position: Using pillows to maintain a neutral spine and reduce nerve tension. * Driving Posture: Adjusting the seat angle to stop the piriformis from compressing the nerve.

Integrating Long Term Prevention

Getting rid of the pain is only half the battle. The other half is ensuring the sciatica does not return the moment you lift something heavy or sit too long on a flight.

Developing a Mobility Maintenance Routine

We provide a custom set of movements that keep the sciatic nerve mobile and the hip joints fluid. These are not just stretches, but functional movements designed to keep the lower back from becoming the primary pivot point of your body.

Weight Management and Joint Load

Excess weight can increase the load on the lumbar spine and the pelvic girdle, increasing the risk of nerve compression. We provide guidance on how to stay active and manage joint load during your recovery process.

FAQs About Sciatica Treatment

 

Why does my pain move from my back to my calf?

This is called "peripheralization." It happens when the nerve irritation increases. When the pain moves back toward the spine, it is called "centralization," which is a sign that the treatment is working and the nerve is decompression.

Can sciatica happen without back pain?

Yes. In cases of Piriformis Syndrome, you may have intense pain in your buttock and leg without any actual pain in your lower back. This is why a professional assessment is critical to find the actual source.

Is it safe to stretch when I have sciatica?

Some stretches can actually pull on an already irritated nerve, making the inflammation worse. For example, a deep hamstring stretch can put too much tension on the sciatic nerve. Always consult with a therapist to learn which stretches are safe for your specific cause of sciatica.

How many sessions will I need to feel better?

Every body is different. Some patients feel a significant drop in pain after 2 or 3 sessions, while chronic cases may take several weeks of consistent work. We set clear milestones at every visit to track your progress.

Can stress make my sciatica worse?

Absolutely. Stress increases muscle tension, particularly in the hips and lower back. It also lowers your pain threshold, making the nerve sensations feel more intense. We focus on the physical side, but we acknowledge the impact of stress on recovery.

What is the difference between a pinched nerve and sciatica?

Sciatica is a specific type of pinched nerve. While you can have a pinched nerve in your wrist or neck, "sciatica" specifically refers to the irritation of the sciatic nerve in the lower body.

Living with the constant threat of a "flare up" is exhausting. You deserve to move without fear and sleep without pain. Our Milton clinic specializes in the precise diagnosis and treatment of sciatic nerve issues. Stop guessing and start healing. Contact Tonic Physio today to schedule your sciatica assessment.

Recover Your Mobility: Expert Herniated Disc Treatment in Milton

A herniated disc can transform a simple movement into a source of intense pain. Whether it is a sharp shooting sensation down your leg or a dull ache in your lower back that prevents you from sleeping, the impact on your daily life is immediate. At Tonic Physio, we focus on reducing the pressure on your nerves and restoring the structural integrity of your spine through targeted, evidence-based care.

Understanding the Mechanics of a Herniated Disc

A herniated disc occurs when the soft, jelly-like center of a spinal disc pushes through a tear in the tougher outer casing. This protrusion can irritate nearby nerves, leading to inflammation, numbness, and severe pain. While many people fear that a herniated disc automatically means surgery, the reality is that the vast majority of cases resolve with a structured physiotherapy program.

Common Symptoms of Disc Herniation

The symptoms vary depending on where the disc is located. In the lumbar region (lower back), you might feel: * Radiating pain that travels through the buttock and down the leg. * Numbness or tingling in the feet or toes. * Muscle weakness in the legs that affects your gait. * Increased pain when sneezing, coughing, or sitting for long periods. In the cervical region (neck), symptoms often include: * Pain that radiates into the shoulder or arm. * Weakness in the grip or hand coordination issues. * Persistent stiffness in the neck and upper trapezius.

Why Early Intervention Matters

Ignoring a herniated disc often leads to compensatory patterns. Your body naturally shifts your weight and posture to avoid pain, which puts undue stress on other joints. This often results in secondary injuries in the hips or opposite side of the back. Starting treatment early prevents these chronic patterns from setting in.

Our Approach to Herniated Disc Recovery at Tonic Physio

We do not believe in a one size fits all approach. Every spine is different, and every injury has a unique trigger. Our Milton clinic uses a combination of manual therapy, corrective exercise, and patient education to create a path toward permanent relief.

Phase 1: Pain Modulation and Inflammation Control

The first goal is to calm the nervous system. When a disc herniates, the surrounding area becomes chemically inflamed. We use specific techniques to reduce this inflammation and centralize the pain. Centralization occurs when pain moves from the extremities (like the foot) back toward the center of the spine, which is a primary indicator of recovery.

Phase 2: Restoring Segmental Mobility

Once the acute pain is managed, we focus on mobility. A herniated disc often leads to "stiffness" in the segments above and below the injury. By improving the mobility of these surrounding joints, we reduce the mechanical load on the damaged disc, allowing it to heal more effectively.

Phase 3: Core Stability and Spinal Support

True recovery happens when your muscles can support your spine. We move beyond basic "core exercises" and focus on deep stabilizers like the multifidus and transversus abdominis. We teach you how to maintain a neutral spine during daily activities, ensuring that you do not re-injure the disc while bending or lifting.

Advanced Techniques for Disc Relief

At Tonic Physio, we integrate modern modalities with traditional manual therapy to accelerate the healing process.

Manual Therapy and Spinal Mobilization

Our therapists use hands-on techniques to gently mobilize the vertebrae. This helps create space for the nerve and encourages the disc material to recede. Unlike aggressive manipulations, our approach is controlled and tailored to your specific pain tolerance.

Targeted Corrective Exercise

Exercise is the most powerful tool for long term spinal health. We design a progression of movements that start with gentle isometric holds and evolve into functional strength training. This ensures your spine is resilient enough to handle the demands of your lifestyle, whether you are an athlete or work a desk job.

Posture Re-Education

Many disc issues are exacerbated by "text neck" or prolonged slouching. We analyze your sitting and standing postures to identify the triggers that compress your discs. By adjusting your ergonomics and movement patterns, we remove the daily stressors that hinder your recovery.

When to Seek Urgent Care

While most herniated discs respond well to physiotherapy, certain symptoms require immediate medical attention. Please contact a physician or visit an emergency room if you experience: * Sudden loss of bowel or bladder control. * "Saddle anesthesia" (numbness in the groin or inner thighs). * Severe, sudden weakness in a limb that prevents you from standing. These can be signs of Cauda Equina Syndrome, a rare but serious condition that requires surgical intervention.

Living With a History of Disc Injury

Recovering from a herniated disc is not just about getting back to zero; it is about becoming more resilient than you were before the injury. Many of our patients find that they have better posture and more strength after completing their program than they did before the disc event occurred.

Maintaining Long Term Spinal Health

Consistency is the key to preventing recurrence. We provide our patients with a lifelong maintenance plan, including: * Daily mobility flows to keep the spine supple. * Strength benchmarks to ensure the core remains supportive. * Ergonomic checklists for home and office environments.

The Role of Nutrition and Hydration

Spinal discs are largely made of water. Dehydration can make discs more brittle and prone to tearing. We encourage our patients to maintain optimal hydration and a nutrient-dense diet to support the collagen structures within the spinal column.

FAQs About Herniated Disc Treatment

 

Do I need an MRI before starting physiotherapy?

Not necessarily. While an MRI provides a clear picture of the disc, many people have disc bulges on an MRI but feel no pain. We treat the symptoms and the functional limitations, not just the image. If your symptoms are atypical, we may suggest imaging to confirm the diagnosis.

How long does it take to recover from a herniated disc?

Recovery timelines vary. Some patients see significant improvement in 2 to 4 weeks, while others may require 3 to 6 months of consistent therapy. The goal is to move from acute pain to functional stability.

Can a herniated disc heal without surgery?

Yes. The body has a natural ability to resorb the protruding disc material over time. Physiotherapy facilitates this process by reducing inflammation and improving the mechanical environment of the spine.

Will I have to stop working during treatment?

In most cases, no. We work with you to modify your activities. If you have a sedentary job, we suggest frequent movement breaks. If you have a physically demanding job, we provide strategies to lift and move safely while you recover.

What is the difference between a bulging disc and a herniated disc?

A bulging disc is when the disc extends beyond its normal space but the outer wall remains intact. A herniated disc occurs when the outer wall actually tears, allowing the inner gel to leak out. Both can cause pain, but herniated discs often cause more acute nerve irritation.

Is stretching the best way to fix a herniated disc?

Not always. Some stretches, like touching your toes, can actually put more pressure on a herniated disc and make the injury worse. We teach you "safe" stretches and movements that decompression the spine rather than compressing it.

Whether you are dealing with a new injury or a chronic disc issue that keeps returning, our team in Milton is ready to help you regain your strength and mobility. Contact Tonic Physio today to schedule your assessment and take the first step toward a pain-free spine.

Understanding the Causes and Signs of Osteoarthritis

FAQs About Osteoarthritis

What causes osteoarthritis?

Over time, as the cushioning wears away, bones begin to rub together, causing stiffness, swelling, and reduced joint mobility. The knees, hips, hands, and spine are often the most affected areas.

Can osteoarthritis be cured?

How can exercise help with osteoarthritis?

FAQs About Tonic Physio & Rehabilitation Centre

Do I need a referral to see a physiotherapist in Canada?

Many patients wonder if a doctor’s referral is required. Generally, no referral is needed, but certain provincial public plans (e.g., OHIP) or insurance providers may require one

Is physiotherapy covered by insurance in Canada?

Coverage varies: public plans (OHIP, seniors, post-discharge) may cover physio, while private insurance often supplements this—check your policy carefully

How long does a typical physiotherapy session last?

Standard sessions are typically 30–60 minutes, depending on the injury or treatment plan

How many physio sessions will I need to recover?

Mild conditions: 2–3 sessions; soft-tissue injuries: 6–8 weeks; complex or chronic issues: 2–4 months

What conditions can physiotherapy treat?

Physio helps with musculoskeletal (back, shoulder, knee), neurological (stroke, MS), cardiopulmonary (post-surgery, COPD), and women’s health issues

Can I combine physiotherapy with massage or chiropractic care?

Yes, integrated treatment plans (e.g. physio + massage) often lead to better outcomes, and many clinics offer direct billing for convenience

What is telehealth physiotherapy, and is it effective?

Tele-rehab uses video sessions to deliver personalized exercise plans remotely. It’s growing in Canada, especially useful for remote areas—though best suited for mild to moderate conditions

Are physiotherapists licensed in Canada?

Yes, practitioners must complete a Master’s degree, pass the Physiotherapy Competency Exam (PCE), and register with their provincial regulatory body

What should I expect during my first physiotherapy visit?

Your therapist will perform a comprehensive assessment (movement, strength, posture) and create a personalized treatment plan, including exercises, manual therapy, and goal-setting.

How long does it take for physiotherapy to work?

While some notice relief after 1–2 sessions, full recovery depends on injury type: soft tissue (~6–8 weeks); chronic conditions may require months of consistent treatment and home exercises .

Shockwave Therapy in Milton

Shockwave Therapy is a non-invasive, clinically proven treatment that uses high-energy acoustic sound waves to treat musculoskeletal conditions and chronic pain. It works by delivering focused shockwaves to painful or injured areas, stimulating the body’s healing response, improving blood circulation, and reducing inflammation.

This advanced therapy is especially effective for soft tissue injuries, tendonitis, and persistent joint pain that hasn’t improved with conventional physiotherapy techniques.

What is Shockwave Therapy?

Shockwave Therapy uses high-frequency acoustic waves delivered through a handheld device. These waves penetrate deeply into affected tissues, helping to break down calcium deposits, relieve muscle tension, and speed up tissue repair.

During a session, a trained therapist uses a stainless steel applicator to deliver precise pulses to targeted areas. This triggers a controlled inflammatory response that boosts collagen production, improves blood flow, and supports long-term healing.

Conditions Treated with Shockwave Therapy

Shockwave physiotherapy is an effective treatment option for a wide range of conditions, including:

  • Plantar fasciitis
  • Achilles tendonitis
  • Tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis)
  • Rotator cuff tendinopathy
  • Calcific shoulder tendonitis
  • Jumper’s knee (patellar tendinopathy)
  • Heel spurs
  • Myofascial pain syndrome
  • Hip bursitis
  • Chronic muscular pain

How Shockwave Therapy Works

The shockwave therapy equipment produces sound waves through a generator, which are transferred through a tube system to a stainless steel applicator. When applied to the skin, these waves penetrate deep into tissues, stimulating cellular regeneration and increasing blood flow to the targeted area.

The waves also interact with fibrotic tissues and calcium deposits, breaking them apart and reducing tension in the surrounding muscles, tendons, and fascia.

Randy Pedersen

Manual Osteopath Pedorthist

After graduating from McMaster University with his Bachelor’s degree in Kinesiology, Randy pursued his interests in human anatomy and movement at George Brown College’s Prosthetics and Orthotics program. This is where he learned the science and the art of assessing and fabricating prosthetic and orthotic (custom orthopaedic bracing) devices for individuals with limb disorders. Building on that background, Randy continued his education in the Pedorthic field and became a Canadian Board Certified Pedorthist or C.Ped(C). They are one of the few healthcare professionals trained in the assessment of lower limb anatomy and muscle and joint function.

Randy was introduced to osteopathy as a healthcare field via his children’s participation in elite sport. He was intrigued with the philosophy of osteopathy and how osteopathic manual practitioners examine and treat the whole body as an inter-related dynamic unit of function—looking for the cause of dysfunction and not just the result or pain. Following his keen interest in osteopathy, Randy attended the 4-year, principles-based Osteopathic program at the Canadian Academy of Osteopathy where he earned his certification as a Master of Practice in Osteopathic Manipulative Science (M.OMSc.) and is OSTCAN certified.

Frequently Asked Questions

FAQs About Registered Massage Therapy​

What is Orthopedic Physiotherapy?

Orthopedic physiotherapy is focused on treating conditions and injuries affecting the bones, joints, muscles, and connective tissues. It includes a range of treatments to help reduce pain, improve movement, and prevent further injury or deterioration.

How can Orthopedic Physiotherapy help me?

Orthopedic physiotherapy can help relieve pain, improve joint and muscle function, and promote healing from injuries or surgeries. It’s particularly effective for treating sprains, fractures, arthritis, and back or neck pain. Physiotherapists use a variety of techniques including manual therapy, exercises, and modalities to improve function and reduce discomfort.

When should I see an Orthopedic Physiotherapist?

You should consult an orthopedic physiotherapist if you are experiencing pain, stiffness, or difficulty with movement in your joints, muscles, or bones. It is also beneficial after surgery, an injury, or for managing chronic conditions like arthritis. Early intervention can help improve recovery time and prevent long-term complications.

What happens during an Orthopedic Physiotherapy session?

During your session, the physiotherapist will assess your condition and create a treatment plan. This typically includes exercises to improve strength, flexibility, and mobility, along with manual therapy techniques to alleviate pain. They may also educate you on posture, ergonomics, and self-care strategies to prevent further injury.

How long will I need Orthopedic Physiotherapy?

The length of treatment depends on your specific condition and recovery goals. Some individuals may need only a few sessions, while others with more complex or chronic conditions may require ongoing treatment. Your physiotherapist will monitor your progress and adjust the plan as needed.
